reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power and speed are both genuine and both show up in the same profile, which is what makes Merrill interesting at 23. His .493 xSLG sits in the top tenth of the league, his 49.4% hard-hit rate matches it, and he's running 29.0 ft/s — that combination is what drives a projection of 27 home runs and 27 stolen bases across 673 plate appearances. The whole thing hinges on contact quality outrunning contact rate, because a 37.3% chase rate and 6.2% walk rate mean the swing decisions aren't pretty. If pitchers keep him chasing and the strikeout rate climbs past its current 24.0%, the .256/.305 slash gets thinner fast and the counting stats soften with it; if he runs the same hard contact without tightening the zone, he's still a 27/27 middle-of-the-order piece who fields his position well.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .408, the barrel rate is 19.3%, and the hard-hit rate is 58.7%, all three maxed at the top of the Statcast scale, and the argument for Wood is basically just those numbers stacked on top of each other. The one genuine tension in the profile is the 28.6% strikeout rate sitting against a 16.4% walk rate: he's drawing walks at an elite clip, but pitchers who find his swing-and-miss can get him without much trouble, because the whiff rate is 30.0%. If the contact rate stays where it is and the zone discipline holds, the projection's .898 OPS and 31 home runs translate to a true middle-of-the-order corner outfielder; if pitchers start burying him in his vulnerable zones and the strikeouts climb without the walks keeping pace, the power and patience are still enough to carry an everyday profile, just at lower wattage.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .297, 99th percentile, while the projection has him at .285, and that gap tells you something useful: the batted-ball quality is running ahead of actual results, which gives the .824 OPS projection a floor more than a ceiling. A 92.9 mph average exit velocity paired with a 53.5% hard-hit rate describes a hitter who punishes contact consistently, not occasionally. Health is the only dependency that matters.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The .406 OBP across AA & A+ & A is the headline, but 95 walks in 538 plate appearances is what makes it stick. Willits is 18 years old drawing walks at a clip that translates to 12.7 BB%, well above where the average big-league hitter lands, and he's stolen 62 bases this season, so the profile isn't just patience — it moves. The ISO translates to .134, a tick below the MLB mean of .150, so the real dependency is whether the power develops enough that pitchers can't simply pitch around him at the next level. If it does, you're looking at an everyday shortstop; if the power stalls, the walk rate and legs still build a useful player, just not the top-of-the-order anchor the ceiling implies.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Chase Burns

reports.name: Henry Bolte
reports.published_report: The loud number is 30.5 ft/s sprint speed, and it's the whole argument for and against him at once. That kind of elite closing speed turns fringe contact into hits and fringe baserunning into 22 projected steals, but a 33.2% whiff rate at the 6th percentile means the contact isn't showing up where it should — his hard-hit rate sits at 48.3% and his exit velocity averages 90.9 mph, yet his xSLG comes out to .373 at the 29th percentile, which tells you the loud contact isn't landing in favorable spots often enough. The projection splits the difference: a .272/.355 line that plays like a second-division regular with genuine stolen-base value, not a gap hitter with upside. If the whiff rate doesn't come down, what's left is a speed-first outfielder whose bat has to borrow credibility from his legs every single day.

reports.name: Francisco Alvarez
reports.published_report: A 15.3% barrel rate at the 96th percentile is an elite contact-quality trait living inside a strikeout problem. The whiff rate sits at 35.2%, and that's where the profile breaks: he's generating elite damage on contact while making contact on only a fraction of swings, which is how you get an xBA of .227 paired with an xSLG of .423, power that reads loud on Statcast but gets buried by the swing-and-miss. If the strikeout rate holds at 30.8%, the projection's .232/.312/.401 line is probably about right for a catcher who barrels the ball at that frequency, and 17 projected home runs across 423 plate appearances undersells what happens if he ever tightens the zone. The whole read hinges on whether he learns to get to that contact more often; if he doesn't, he's a high-variance regular whose best games look like a middle-of-the-order bat and whose worst stretches look like a lineup drain.

reports.name: Tyler Soderstrom
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball hasn't arrived yet, but the plate discipline is already there. Soderstrom's 11.7% walk rate sits well above league norms, and he pairs it with a 25.9% chase rate that says the zone management is genuine, not passive, because the 90.7 mph average exit velo and 45.4% hard-hit rate confirm he's swinging with intent when he does engage. The xwOBA of .328 and xSLG of .411 land in the middle of the pack, which is the honest picture: a left-side-of-average hitter by expected outcomes who gets to 19 projected home runs through volume contact and real power when he connects. If the actual batting average creeps toward the xBA of .246 rather than the .245 projection, this is a useful everyday corner bat; if the contact quality uptick in the projection never materializes, he's a well-disciplined second-division regular with above-average walk totals and a floor that the fielding grade makes uninspiring.

reports.name: Jake Bauers
reports.published_report: The .380 xwOBA sits in the 97th percentile, which is the whole tension here: a guy who makes almost no contact when pitchers attack the zone but damages everything he does reach. Bauers chases just 21.3% of pitches outside the zone and draws walks at a 16.8% clip that almost nobody in the league matches, so his .395 OBP projection isn't wishful — it's the discipline carrying him to first base on pitches he never swings at. The 14.2% barrel rate and 52.6% hard-hit rate explain the projected .494 SLG; this is a man who hits the ball extremely hard when he hits it, and the expected numbers say he's been doing it consistently enough to trust. The entire profile hinges on whether that 25.9% strikeout rate stays manageable, because if pitchers find a way to exploit the 29.0% whiff rate and he stops making the walks count, you're looking at a limited platoon piece rather than a near-.900 OPS corner bat.

reports.name: Coby Mayo
reports.published_report: The power profile is legitimate and the hit tool is the problem. Mayo's 13.5% barrel rate and 91.3 mph average exit velocity translate to an .478 xSLG, the kind of raw thump that makes 25 home runs in 457 plate appearances entirely plausible. If he tightens his whiff rate enough to keep pitchers from burying him, he's a low-end everyday corner bat with real pop; if the strikeout hole stays where it is, the .227 average in the projection becomes the ceiling, not the floor, and he slides toward a platoon role where the thump-to-contact tradeoff is at least manageable.

Henderson gets hitters out the old-fashioned way: he doesn't walk them, and at 30.7% he strikes out nearly a third of the batters he faces, all without elite velocity at 93.1 mph. The barrel rate (8.9%) is the one number that gives pause, sitting in the bottom quarter of the league, meaning when contact does happen, it tends to count. If the control slips or hitters start timing him without that premium fastball, the barrel rate becomes the story; as long as it holds, this profile projects to a legitimate frontline starter.

reports.name: Zyhir Hope
reports.published_report: Twenty-nine home runs and 26 stolen bases at AA, age 21, is the kind of line that makes you sit up — and then you look at the translation and the sit-up becomes a squint. The raw power translates to a .166 ISO against MLB pitching, which clears the MLB average of .150, but the 27% strikeout rate against that same competition is the thing the whole profile hangs on. Hope has 62 walks in 564 AA plate appearances to cushion the contact risk, and he's punishing mistakes when he connects, but if the strikeout rate doesn't compress as pitchers get sharper, the hit tool erodes and you're left with a power/speed corner bat who can't stay in the lineup every day. Either a second-division regular with impact tool flashes, or a bench piece riding the tools he has right now.

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero

Eduardo Quintero is 20, posting a 17% walk rate that translates to 12.6% at the MLB level, well above the league mean, and 44 stolen bases give him a real dimension beyond the bat. The power is the honest concern: a .191 ISO in the minors translates to .135 at the big-league level, below average, so what he becomes depends almost entirely on whether the hit tool and speed carry enough value to cover that gap. If they do, he's a table-setter who gets on base at a high clip; if the contact slips even a little against better arms, a bench outfielder is the ceiling.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The 3.59 ERA projection is doing Weathers a favor, and the Statcast profile explains why. His xERA sits at 4.28 with an xwOBA of .319, both in the bottom third of the league, and hitters are making hard contact at a 40.6% clip — his control is the one thing holding this together. At 6.7% walks with 25.2% strikeouts, the command-to-stuff ratio is genuinely inverted from what you want in a rotation piece: he limits free passes, but he isn't missing bats at a rate that punishes the contact he allows. If the control slips even modestly, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, and a starter posting an xERA like that becomes a reliever-by-necessity story pretty quickly.

reports.name: Liam Hicks

Across AA & A+, Bitonti has put up a .245 ISO and drawn 82 walks against 172 strikeouts in 517 plate appearances — that's a 33% strikeout rate that translates to 35.9% against big-league pitching, while the MLB average sits at 22.0%. The walk rate is genuine separation, translating to 11.8% in an MLB context, but everything hinges on whether the swing-and-miss tightens even modestly as he climbs, because a 1B-only profile at 35.9% K% doesn't leave a roster much margin to carry him. If the contact rate moves even a little, there's a solid regular here; if it doesn't, the floor is a bench piece who gets spotted against righties and lives on his .378 OBP days.

What saves him from being a flat no is a 17.0% strikeout rate that most guys with this kind of contact quality can't post, plus legitimate speed at 28.5 ft/s. 14.8% barrel rate. That's the whole engine, and it's a 95th-percentile engine sitting inside a profile that otherwise wants to fall apart.

Raleigh chases at 36.1% and whiffs at 31.9%, which drags his xBA to .190 and pulls his K% to 31.6% — the contact picture is genuinely bad. What keeps him afloat is that when he does make contact, it's often the damaging kind, and a 13.2% walk rate that grades near the top of the league gives him enough of a floor that the projection lands at .295 OBP despite the batting average wreckage. The ValuCast projection: 24 home runs across 533 plate appearances with a .675 OPS, which is a second-division regular's output at the plate for a catcher who earns his roster spot behind the dish more than in the box score. If the chase rate ever tightens even modestly, the barrel quality turns him into a genuinely dangerous offensive catcher; if it stays at 36.1%, he's a power-first fringe regular whose value lives entirely in the positional adjustment.

reports.name: Dante Nori
reports.published_report: Contact is the carry tool. Across AA & A+ & A in 2026, Nori has struck out just 53 times in 326 plate appearances, and that 16% clip translates to a 20.0% MLB-equivalent rate, a tick below what the average big-leaguer posts. The problem is everything that contact has to carry: his ISO sits at .109 across those levels, and the MLB translation pegs power at .108, well short of the .150 MLB average, which means the bat's value lives almost entirely in his ability to put the ball in play and move around the bases rather than do damage, and he has 17 stolen bases across the combined line to lean on. If the plate discipline sharpens and the batted-ball quality ticks up, he's a usable bench piece with speed and a glove in center; if the power floor doesn't change and the .311 OBP doesn't grow, the ceiling is organizational depth and nothing more.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the tell: 33.1% gets hitters to expand, and a 27.6% whiff rate does the damage once they do. What the Statcast profile says about Drohan is that he's a pitch-mover more than a pure power arm, using 2443 rpm of fastball spin to make his heater play up past what 94.9 mph would suggest on its own. The barrel rate at 8.8% is the one genuine red flag, sitting well below the league median, and if that contact profile slips the xERA of 3.82 won't hold against a projected 4.25. Either a back-end starter worth streaming in the right matchup or a leveraged reliever with a role problem, depending entirely on whether Milwaukee commits to giving him rotation innings.

reports.name: JJ Bleday
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the load-bearing wall. At 13.5% BB%, Bleday sits in genuinely elite territory for a hitter, and that discipline is what props a .325 OBP onto a .216 projected average. The xwOBA of .340 and the 9.7% barrel rate say the power has shape behind it, but the 23.0% chase rate is the real engine here — he simply doesn't give away at-bats, and pitchers who try to work around him pay for it over 549 projected plate appearances. The profile resolves into an everyday outfielder if the .216 average doesn't drag the lineup down enough to force a platoon conversation, and into a good bench bat with pop if it does.

reports.name: Bryant Betancourt
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power combination here is the real argument: a 14% strikeout rate across AAA & AA that translates to 17.9% against big-league pitching, well below a league average sitting around 22%, paired with a .21 ISO and 17 home runs in 422 plate appearances at those levels. The translation puts his walk rate right at the margin, 8.0% against an MLB average of 8.5%, which means the profile is contact-and-power first with discipline as a quiet asset, not the other way around. He's a catcher, and catchers with this kind of bat-to-ball profile and double-digit power tend to land on a roster in some capacity — the question is volume, and whether the glove earns him the everyday job or pushes him toward a bench role where that .334 OBP quietly underperforms his bat. Either a low-end regular or a useful platoon piece behind the plate, with the floor being bench depth if the glove doesn't hold at the highest level.

reports.name: Andrés Giménez
reports.published_report: A 3.2% barrel rate and a 43.9% chase rate in the same profile tells you almost everything. Giménez is making contact at a decent clip, 18.5% strikeouts is fine, but he's expanding the zone at a rate that lands in the 2nd percentile, and when he does make contact, 85.3 mph average exit velocity and 24.7% hard-hit rate say the ball just doesn't travel. The projection's .288 OBP and .645 OPS across 520 PA reflect that honestly: the speed (21 projected steals) and elite-caliber defense keep him on the field, but the offensive floor is a second-division regular who needs the stolen bases to matter in the lineup context around him. If the chase rate doesn't come down, there's no bat-speed floor to catch the fall.

reports.name: Jarren Duran
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are the problem. Duran's Statcast profile is a study in contradiction: 89.7 mph average exit velocity and a 9.4% barrel rate suggest a hitter who hits the ball hard enough when he connects, but a 33.8% whiff rate and 34.6% chase rate mean he connects far less often than a lineup regular can afford. The expected numbers settle the argument — his .298 xwOBA and .234 xBA aren't a slump, they're what the swing produces, and the projection's .206 AVG and .264 OBP over 622 plate appearances translates that honestly. What makes the profile survivable at all is 29.0 ft/s sprint speed, which keeps him dangerous on the bases and in center field, but speed doesn't fix a strikeout profile that lives in the bottom tier of the league.

reports.name: Dylan Crews
reports.published_report: The contact and walk rates are the problem. A 29.9% whiff rate and 6.6% walk rate leave almost no margin for the exit velocity to matter, and the current .223/.289 projection line shows exactly what happens when good contact quality meets poor plate discipline — you get a league-average xSLG of .419 that never translates into production because the at-bats that don't end in strikeouts don't generate enough baserunners to leverage it. The one loud, unambiguous tool is the sprint speed: 29.3 ft/s puts him in the 94th percentile, and that plus the 9.5% barrel rate give him a real floor as a capable-enough outfielder who adds a few stolen bases. If the chase rate comes down and he starts making the 90.0 mph average exit velocity count in more plate appearances, there's a second-division regular in there; if the whiff and walk numbers stay where they are, he settles in as a fringe bench piece whose speed is the only thing keeping him rostered.

reports.name: Marcus Phillips
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the command is the problem, and right now the problem is winning. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Translate that profile to MLB-equivalent and the strikeouts land near league average while the walk rate lands at 6.4, roughly double what big-league starters typically allow, and a K-BB% of 8.6% against the 13.5% norm tells you exactly how much the free passes are eating the upside. The entire profile hinges on whether the walks compress as he matures, because if they don't, the strikeout ceiling has nowhere to go and he's a depth arm by ceiling and floor.

The profile hinges on whether the command tightens as he climbs, because if it doesn't, the swing-and-miss just pays rent on the walks instead of building anything, and the ceiling here is a depth arm either way.
